title: Lifespan Development: Theory, Context, and Research Interpretation
scope_note: Original review of lifespan developmental principles, major theoretical perspectives, research design, and evidence limits. Scope is limited to the linked official board outline and curriculum references; this is not an exam prediction.
learning_objectives: Compare continuous and stage-oriented accounts without treating either as universal.
Interpret findings in biological, cognitive, social, and cultural context.
Distinguish longitudinal, cross-sectional, and correlational evidence and their limits.

sections.heading: 1. Development across domains and time
sections.body: Development describes patterned change and continuity across the lifespan. Physical, cognitive, language, emotional, and social processes interact; a change in one domain may affect opportunities in another. A lifespan view considers gains, losses, context, and individual variation rather than assuming that all change ends in childhood. Milestones organize questions but do not establish an individual diagnosis or a fixed timetable.
items: Specify the domain and age period.
Separate general patterns from claims about one person.
Consider setting and opportunity.

sections.heading: 2. Theories and developmental mechanisms
sections.body: Theories offer different explanations for change. Continuous accounts emphasize gradual accumulation, while stage accounts propose qualitative reorganizations in some capacities. Learning, cognition, attachment, maturation, and sociocultural participation highlight different mechanisms. Apply a theory to the evidence supplied; do not convert a broad framework into a guaranteed age-specific rule.
items: Identify the mechanism a theory emphasizes.
Match the framework to the described observation.
State what the framework does not establish.

sections.heading: 3. Nature, experience, and variation
sections.body: Development reflects interactions among biological conditions, experience, relationships, and environments. A shared exposure can have different effects because learners and contexts differ. An association between an experience and an outcome does not identify causation, direction, or mechanism by itself. Avoid deterministic claims from a single characteristic or exposure; describe evidence and uncertainty carefully.
items: Separate exposure from measured outcome.
Consider timing, individual variation, and other explanations.
Do not infer causation from one association.

sections.heading: 4. Research design and ethics
sections.body: Longitudinal research follows the same participants and can observe within-person change, but attrition, repeated testing, and historical change matter. Cross-sectional research compares groups at one time and is efficient, but age can be confounded with cohort and period. Correlational research estimates association rather than causal effect. Research with children and families requires consent, privacy, risk management, and review.
items: Name who is measured and when.
Identify cohort, attrition, and measurement limits.
Apply the relevant participant protections.

worked_examples.heading: Compare age groups cautiously
worked_examples.prompt: Two age groups take a language measure in different years, after one cohort experienced extended school closures. What can be inferred from a score difference?
steps: Report the observed difference between the tested groups.
Recognize that age and historical opportunity vary together.
Avoid attributing the difference to age alone without a design that separates those explanations.
worked_examples.answer: The groups differ on this measure in this setting; the data do not isolate an age effect.
worked_examples.check: The inference does not exceed the cross-sectional evidence.

common_misconceptions: A milestone is an exact deadline for every child.
A stage theory explains every domain and individual equally.
An association proves a developmental cause.
Longitudinal findings cannot be affected by cohort change or attrition.
question_patterns: Choose a design for the change question.
Interpret observations with context and limits.
Compare theoretical explanations without treating them as universal laws.

title: Architectural Practice, Coordination, and Public Responsibility
scope_note: The PRC architecture syllabus includes principles of planning and architectural practice. Republic Act 9266 describes the statutory scope of architecture services. This lesson teaches bounded project reasoning and source checking; it is not a legal opinion, current-code determination, or exam prediction.
learning_objectives: Relate a project task to the documented service scope, role, and decision record.
Trace a coordination issue from its source through responsible review and a controlled revision.
Use current official safety and accessibility references when a decision affects the public.

sections.heading: 1. Practice scope and service responsibilities
sections.body: Architectural practice joins site and planning work, design, documentation, coordination, and construction-related services. Read the engagement as a defined professional service: identify the client, deliverables, responsible signatory, review boundaries, and decisions that require another qualified discipline. Republic Act 9266 is a primary Philippine reference for regulated scope; its text should be checked directly, together with current implementing rules, before a regulatory conclusion is made. In a project case, separate what the architect is responsible for from what a consultant, contractor, approving office, or client controls. A clear service record helps prevent a drawing or verbal instruction from silently expanding the assignment. It does not remove duties imposed by applicable law or professional standards.

sections.heading: 2. Coordinate decisions across project information
sections.body: A coordination problem often appears as conflicting information across drawings, specifications, site observations, and consultant inputs. First identify the exact location and revision of each record. State the discrepancy without assigning cause, identify which discipline or decision-maker owns the next review, and preserve the response in a dated issue log. The resolved direction must be carried into the controlled documents and communicated to affected participants. A meeting note alone is not proof that every drawing was updated. Check that the current set has a common revision status, that superseded information is identifiable, and that unresolved items remain visible. Escalate a conflict that affects safety, compliance, cost, or scope instead of filling the gap with an unsupported assumption.

sections.heading: 3. Public responsibility, safety, and access
sections.body: Professional decisions can affect people who did not commission the project: occupants, neighbors, workers, and visitors. Identify who may be excluded or exposed to risk by the proposed arrangement, then consult the current official requirements and responsible specialists. For accessibility, verify the applicable law, rules, building use, route, and project conditions rather than relying on a single remembered dimension. For safety, communicate unresolved hazards and assign a responsible review before work proceeds. A useful decision note records the evidence considered, the people affected, the applicable source checked, the responsible reviewer, and the action taken. An architect can explain design reasoning but should not present an unverified code interpretation as a final determination.

sections.heading: 4. Worked case: a conflicting service route
sections.body: A reflected ceiling plan shows a service route passing through a structural member, while the latest structural sheet shows the member in that location. The project team should preserve both drawing references and revisions, describe the physical conflict, and issue it to the responsible architecture and engineering reviewers. Do not move the route on an uncontrolled sheet or assume that the smaller system can be shifted without checking access and maintenance. Once the authorized design direction is recorded, update the coordinated sheets, identify the superseded revision, and notify the affected site team. The check is complete only when the resolution is visible in the current coordinated set.

sections.heading: 5. Review: a defensible project decision
sections.body: Before closing a practice problem, ask: What is the exact issue? Which source and revision establish it? Who has authority and competence to decide? What public or project risk follows from delay? Where will the decision be recorded? Which controlled documents must change? Use these questions to distinguish a traceable professional decision from an informal assumption.

worked_examples.heading: Resolve a document conflict
worked_examples.prompt: An architectural plan and a consultant schedule give different locations for a building service. The site team asks which one to follow.
steps: Record both document names, revision dates, and the exact location.
Send the issue to the responsible design reviewers and identify any safety or access consequence.
Record the approved direction, revise the coordinated set, and notify affected participants.
worked_examples.answer: Hold the conflicting work at the affected location until the responsible review is documented, then coordinate the controlled revision.
worked_examples.check: The current drawings and the issue log should show the same resolved location; an untracked verbal instruction is not enough.

worked_examples.heading: Check a service boundary
worked_examples.prompt: A client asks for an extra site and permit deliverable that is not listed in the signed scope.
steps: Identify the requested deliverable and its decision deadline.
Check the written service agreement, statutory obligations, and which qualified professional is responsible.
Document any agreed scope change and its effects on fee, schedule, coordination, and approvals.
worked_examples.answer: Clarify responsibility and document an authorized scope change before treating the extra deliverable as included.
worked_examples.check: A scope record does not override duties set by applicable law or professional standards.

common_misconceptions: A verbal decision automatically updates all controlled drawings.
A coordination issue belongs only to the discipline whose drawing first showed it.
A remembered code value can substitute for checking the current official rule and project context.
A written service agreement removes every statutory or public-safety duty.
question_patterns: Identify the responsible scope, record, and reviewer in a project scenario.
Trace a coordination discrepancy through controlled resolution and communication.
Choose what must be verified before making a safety or accessibility claim.

title: Architectural Precedent, Context, and Conservation
scope_note: The PRC architecture syllabus includes history and theory of architecture, including the influence of environmental, historical, and sociocultural factors. Republic Act 9266 includes conservation and restoration in its architecture-practice scope. The National Park Service references here are instructional conservation and documentation guidance, not Philippine law.
learning_objectives: Compare architectural precedents using form, use, time, place, and source evidence.
Explain how climate and sociocultural context may influence building form without treating one feature as universal proof.
Plan a documented conservation response that distinguishes significance, observed condition, and proposed intervention.

sections.heading: 1. Read precedent as evidence
sections.body: A precedent is useful when its features are connected to a particular time, place, use, and body of evidence. Begin with a reliable plan, section, photograph, written account, or measured survey. Describe what can be observed before assigning a style or influence. Compare spatial organization, materials, structure, circulation, and intended use, then ask which historical or social conditions help explain the differences. Similar forms do not prove direct borrowing, and a label does not explain how a building worked. Keep observations, source claims, and interpretation distinct. This method supports critical comparison rather than memorizing isolated names and dates.

sections.heading: 2. Vernacular form, climate, and use
sections.body: Buildings respond to weather, materials, construction knowledge, household or community practice, and available resources. Test a climate explanation against multiple pieces of evidence: orientation, openings, shading, rain protection, material behavior, local conditions, and the way people use the space. A feature may serve more than one purpose, and similar forms can arise in different places for different reasons. Avoid treating “vernacular” as a single timeless style or assigning one environmental cause without evidence. Describe the site and climate conditions, compare examples, and state the limits of the inference. This approach connects architectural form with environmental and sociocultural context while respecting local variation.

sections.heading: 3. Conservation begins with significance and condition
sections.body: Before proposing a repair or alteration, establish what is significant, what is physically observed, and what evidence is still missing. A photograph or survey documents condition at a point in time; it does not by itself diagnose the cause of deterioration. Record material, location, extent, prior alterations, and safety concerns. Consult appropriate specialists and the relevant current Philippine authority when a project may be regulated. Conservation guidance emphasizes understanding and documenting a historic property before choosing treatment. For examination reasoning, distinguish stabilizing an immediate risk, repairing a diagnosed problem, rehabilitating use, restoring a documented earlier state, and reconstructing missing fabric; do not assume they are interchangeable.

sections.heading: 4. Worked comparison: form and climate
sections.body: Two coastal buildings both use broad roof overhangs. One has deep verandas and cross-ventilation; the other has a protected service gallery and a different orientation. The shared roof feature alone does not prove a common historical source or identical climate strategy. Compare each site’s sun and rain exposure, program, construction, chronology, and use evidence. The defensible conclusion may be that the feature has a plausible environmental role in each case while the broader design responds to different conditions. Keep the claim proportional to the evidence.

sections.heading: 5. Worked case: a historic building leak
sections.body: A historic public building leaks at one roof junction, and a proposal would replace the entire roof profile. First document the location, weather conditions, materials, visible damage, and any immediate risk to occupants. Review available drawings and repair history; have an appropriately qualified specialist investigate the cause. Compare a targeted repair with broader alternatives against significance, performance, safety, and documented evidence. If intervention is justified, state what will change, why, and how the work will be recorded. Do not infer that age alone proves the original roof should be replaced.

worked_examples.heading: Compare two precedents
worked_examples.prompt: Two buildings share a courtyard form but differ in date, climate, material, and community use. What can a comparison reasonably establish?
steps: Describe the courtyard and its relationship to rooms, circulation, and surrounding space in each case.
Check chronology, local environmental conditions, construction evidence, and documented use.
State which similarities are observable and which explanations remain interpretations.
worked_examples.answer: The comparison can identify shared spatial features and evidence-supported differences; it cannot establish direct influence from form alone.
worked_examples.check: A defensible interpretation names its sources and avoids turning a visual resemblance into a historical fact.

worked_examples.heading: Choose a conservation next step
worked_examples.prompt: A measured drawing shows a crack in historic masonry, but no record explains when it formed or whether it is active.
steps: Record location, dimensions, material, and conditions with dated images or survey notes.
Check earlier documentation and obtain appropriate structural or conservation assessment if safety or stability may be affected.
Compare intervention options after significance, cause, and risk are understood.
worked_examples.answer: Document and assess the condition before selecting a repair, while addressing any immediate safety risk through qualified review.
worked_examples.check: A visible symptom is not a diagnosis; treatment should follow evidence about cause and significance.

common_misconceptions: A recognizable style label explains the building’s historical development.
One feature proves a single climate cause or direct cultural influence.
A photograph documents the cause of deterioration rather than the observed condition.
Replacing old material is automatically safer or more historically accurate.
question_patterns: Interpret a precedent with chronology, site, use, material, and source evidence.
Compare environmental responses without treating a feature as universal proof.
Select a documented and proportionate next step for a conservation case.

title: Applied Civil Engineering: Models, Surveying, Transport, and Construction
scope_note: The March 2026 PRC CELE program identifies applied mathematics, engineering data, surveying and layout, transportation/highways, quantity surveying, construction safety, and construction management. This original guide teaches selected shared methods and is not a complete CE reviewer or a substitute for current project specifications.
learning_objectives: Translate an engineering situation into a dimensional model and check the result.
Explain how field observations, quantities, and assumptions affect a construction decision.
Use a transparent comparison before recommending a transport or project action.

sections.heading: 1. Models, units, and engineering data
sections.body: A quantitative result is meaningful only when the model matches the question and every quantity has compatible units. Start by sketching the physical situation, naming knowns and unknowns, and writing the governing relationship before substituting numbers. Convert units before arithmetic, carry units through intermediate steps, and estimate the order of magnitude. Engineering data also need context: sample size, measurement method, spread, and the conditions under which observations were collected. A precise calculation based on a wrong model or unrepresentative data is still a poor decision.

sections.heading: 2. Surveying, layout, and quantities
sections.body: Surveying turns a reference system and field observations into positions, elevations, distances, and layout decisions. A level loop should close against a known benchmark or another defensible check; a closure difference is evidence to investigate, not a value to hide by arbitrary adjustment. For quantity work, define the measurement boundary, units, drawing revision, and assumptions before multiplying dimensions. Reconcile field conditions with the controlled plans and record the source of each quantity. Measurement uncertainty, waste allowances, and pay-item rules must be distinguished rather than blended into one unexplained factor.

sections.heading: 3. Transportation and construction decisions
sections.body: Transportation questions connect movement, capacity, travel time, safety, and land use. Compare alternatives with the same time period and denominator: a count is not a rate, and an average can conceal variation by location or time. Construction planning similarly aligns work sequence, labor and equipment, materials, inspection points, and hazards. Identify the activity, exposure, and people affected before choosing a control; do not treat a checklist as proof that a hazard is controlled. Current law, contract requirements, and site conditions govern actual work.

sections.heading: 4. Cost, schedule, and a defensible recommendation
sections.body: A project comparison should state the alternatives, service period, included costs, assumptions, and any constraints that change the result. Present value, equivalent worth, or a simple payback comparison can support a decision, but none removes uncertainty about demand, maintenance, or delivery risk. A schedule is a network of precedence relationships and durations; a critical path identifies activities whose delay can move the completion date under the modeled logic. Update assumptions when actual progress differs, preserve the reason for a change, and avoid reporting a forecast as a guaranteed finish date.

worked_examples.heading: Check a dimensional model
worked_examples.prompt: A simply supported beam has span 4 m, center load 8 kN, E = 200 GPa, and I = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m⁴. Using the supplied relation δ = PL³/(48EI), find midspan deflection.
steps: Convert P to 8,000 N and E to 200 × 10⁹ N/m²; keep L in metres and I in m⁴.
Convert metres to millimetres by multiplying by 1,000.
worked_examples.answer: Approximately 1.78 mm under the stated idealized model.
worked_examples.check: The dimensional reduction is metres; this is a model result, not a design acceptance check.

common_misconceptions: Unit cancellation is optional in a calculation.
Survey closure error should be hidden rather than investigated and reported.
A critical-path forecast guarantees project completion on that date.
question_patterns: Draw and label a model before calculating.
State a field measurement check and the record it depends on.
Compare project alternatives on a consistent basis.

title: Civil Engineering Hydraulics and Geotechnical Reasoning
scope_note: The current PRC CELE program lists fluid properties and flow, hydrostatics, water supply, soil classification, seepage, soil strength, bearing, compaction, settlement, earth pressure, and slope stability. This guide teaches core reasoning and selected calculations; project design requires site data, applicable standards, and qualified review.
learning_objectives: Distinguish pressure, force, head, and flow using units.
Explain effective stress and why drainage conditions matter.
Estimate a footing area from the allowable pressure explicitly supplied in a problem.

sections.heading: 1. Fluid pressure, head, and flow
sections.body: For a static fluid of constant density, gauge pressure increases with depth according to p = ρgh; absolute pressure adds the local atmospheric pressure. Pressure is force per area, while hydraulic head expresses energy per unit weight as a length. For steady incompressible flow in a closed system, continuity relates discharge to area and average velocity, Q = AV. Bernoulli-type energy accounting also requires the correct elevation, pressure, velocity, pump, turbine, and loss terms. The simplified relations are useful only when their assumptions fit the flow; real channels and networks require appropriate resistance and boundary information.

sections.heading: 2. Soil phases, water, and effective stress
sections.body: Soil behavior depends on the relationships among solids, water, and air, not on a single label such as sand or clay. Water content, void ratio, degree of saturation, and unit weight describe different properties and must not be substituted for one another. For saturated soil under the usual soil-mechanics convention, effective stress σ′ = σ − u, where σ is total stress and u is pore-water pressure. Changes in pore pressure can therefore change the stress carried by the soil skeleton even when the overlying load is unchanged. The convention and drainage conditions should be stated before interpreting strength or settlement.

sections.heading: 3. Bearing, settlement, and slope stability
sections.body: Bearing checks begin with a clearly defined load and contact area; q = P/A gives average contact pressure only for the assumed distribution. An allowable pressure already embeds assumptions supplied by the problem or governing geotechnical report, so it is not a universal soil constant. Settlement is a deformation problem whose magnitude and time depend on compressibility, drainage path, and stress change. Lateral earth pressure and slope stability likewise depend on geometry, water, soil strength, and construction sequence. Distinguish an ultimate failure calculation from a serviceability limit and do not infer site capacity from a classroom example.

sections.heading: 4. Investigation, compaction, and interpretation
sections.body: A soil description is a hypothesis supported by sampling, testing, and field observations. Classification organizes material using observed and measured properties; it does not replace a strength or compressibility test for a design decision. Compaction changes density by reducing air voids, and the useful moisture-density relationship is established through a stated test method. For seepage, identify the hydraulic boundary and flow path before applying a gradient or discharge model. Record test method, sample disturbance, groundwater conditions, and limitations so another engineer can see how the interpretation was reached.

worked_examples.heading: Estimate a footing area
worked_examples.prompt: A footing carries 900 kN on soil with an allowable bearing pressure of 150 kPa. What minimum plan area follows from the stated average-pressure model?
steps: Use q = P/A and rearrange A = P/q.
Remember 1 kPa = 1 kN/m², so A = 900 kN ÷ 150 kN/m².
Check that force divided by pressure leaves square metres.
worked_examples.answer: 6 m² minimum area under the supplied allowable-pressure assumption.
worked_examples.check: This does not determine shape, eccentricity, settlement, depth, or code compliance.

common_misconceptions: Total stress and effective stress always change together by the same amount.
A problem’s allowable pressure is universally valid for another site.
A soil classification alone proves settlement or slope safety.
question_patterns: Write the assumed water condition before using a pressure relation.
Keep total stress, pore pressure, and effective stress separate.
Check the model limit before turning a calculated value into a design conclusion.

title: Structural Equilibrium, Member Response, and Design Evidence
scope_note: PRC lists engineering mechanics, strength of materials, theory of structures, reinforced-concrete and prestressed members, steel members and connections, footings, construction-material testing, and governing codes. The examples here teach analysis principles; they do not provide current member capacities or code design limits.
learning_objectives: Use equilibrium to check reactions for a simply supported beam.
Relate load, section properties, stress, and deformation within stated assumptions.
Trace a load path and distinguish analysis from code-based design.

sections.heading: 1. Equilibrium before member formulas
sections.body: A structure is in static equilibrium when the sum of forces and moments is zero in the chosen coordinate system. Draw a free-body diagram that isolates the member and shows applied actions, support reactions, distances, and sign convention. Solve independent equilibrium equations, then substitute the reactions back into them as a check. Symmetry can simplify a result only when geometry and loading are actually symmetric. A correct reaction calculation is a boundary condition for later shear and moment analysis; it does not establish that the member is adequately sized.

sections.heading: 2. Stress, section properties, and deformation
sections.body: For a prismatic elastic member under idealized axial load, average normal stress is P/A. In elementary elastic bending, the flexure relation σ = My/I connects bending moment, distance from the neutral axis, and section second moment of area. Deflection formulas require their stated support, load, geometry, and linear-elastic assumptions. Use consistent force and length units, and check whether the requested output is stress, force, or displacement. A formula is not a substitute for checking stability, shear, serviceability, connection behavior, or applicable design provisions.

sections.heading: 3. Load path, structural systems, and materials
sections.body: Loads move through connected members to supports and foundations. At each interface, identify the action transferred, the connection that carries it, and the next resisting element. Reinforced concrete relies on composite action between concrete and reinforcement; steel framing depends on member and connection behavior; prestressing introduces a deliberate force state that changes service response. Material tests provide measured evidence under a method and specimen condition; results should be interpreted with the test’s limits. Do not infer a full structural capacity from one material property or one isolated member calculation.

sections.heading: 4. From analysis to design review
sections.body: Design requires the applicable current code, load combinations, material specifications, detailing rules, and project conditions. A classroom analysis can expose an equilibrium error or explain a member response, but it cannot certify compliance. Track code edition and project jurisdiction, check assumptions against the drawings, and seek the responsible professional review when the model or loading is uncertain. Independent checks should target likely failure paths: units, sign convention, support conditions, section axis, load combinations, and whether a reported demand and capacity use compatible definitions.

worked_examples.heading: Find the reactions of a symmetric beam
worked_examples.prompt: A simply supported beam carries a 10 kN point load at midspan over a 6 m span. Find each support reaction.
steps: Draw the free-body diagram with vertical reactions RA and RB.
Use vertical equilibrium: RA + RB − 10 = 0 kN.
Take moments about A: RB(6) − 10(3) = 0, so RB = 5 kN; then RA = 5 kN.
worked_examples.answer: Each support reaction is 5 kN upward.
worked_examples.check: The reactions sum to 10 kN and their moments balance about either support.

common_misconceptions: A symmetric answer is justified when the loading or supports are not symmetric.
Passing an equilibrium check proves the member is safe.
A material test value is itself a design resistance.
question_patterns: Sketch the free body and sign convention before solving.
Check force and moment balance independently.
Name the code and assumptions needed before claiming a design result.

title: Civil Service Analytical Ability: Assumptions, Logic, and Evidence
scope_note: The CSC examination scope covers analytical ability through assumptions and conclusions, logic, word relationships, and data interpretation. This lesson teaches general reasoning methods using original examples; it does not reproduce or predict CSC examination items.
learning_objectives: Separate a claim from the assumption it needs.
Test whether a conclusion follows from stated conditions.
Read comparisons and data without making unsupported causal claims.

sections.heading: 1. Claims, assumptions, and evidence
sections.body: A conclusion is the claim an argument asks you to accept; premises are the reasons offered for it. An assumption is an unstated bridge that must hold for the reasons to support the conclusion. To find it, ask what must be true for the proposed action to work, then test a counterexample. Prefer a necessary, modest assumption over an attractive extra claim. Evidence that two events occurred together supports a description of association, not automatically a causal explanation. Identify alternative causes, changes in measurement, and who entered the comparison before accepting a causal conclusion.

sections.heading: 2. Conditional rules and categories
sections.body: Translate “if P, then Q” as a one-way rule: P is sufficient for Q, and Q is necessary for P. From P you may infer Q; from not-Q you may infer not-P. Q by itself does not prove P, and not-P does not prove not-Q. For category statements, track “all,” “none,” and “some” precisely. “Some” guarantees at least one, not most or all. In a syllogism, test whether the conclusion follows in every case allowed by the premises rather than relying on a familiar real-world association.

sections.heading: 3. Relationships, sequences, and transformations
sections.body: A word analogy is a relation between pairs, not a test of whether two words feel similar. State the relation in a short sentence—such as tool-to-purpose or part-to-whole—then check that it works in the same direction for the second pair. For a number or symbol sequence, test simple differences, ratios, alternating groups, and consistent positional operations. A good rule explains every supplied term with few exceptions. Avoid overfitting one transition or changing rules mid-sequence to force a preferred answer.

sections.heading: 4. Data interpretation and comparison
sections.body: Before comparing figures, identify the unit, denominator, time window, and group being measured. Counts and rates answer different questions; a larger count may simply reflect a larger population. For a change, calculate the difference and choose the stated baseline before calculating a percentage. Check whether a chart’s scale starts at zero or whether categories overlap. State what the data show, what they do not show, and what additional comparison would be needed to support a causal or generalized conclusion.

worked_examples.heading: Find the needed assumption
worked_examples.prompt: A city should add a pedestrian crossing near the school because many learners cross there. Which assumption supports the proposal?
steps: Identify the proposed action: provide a crossing near the school.
Ask what condition makes that location relevant to the action.
Check the option against the premise without adding an unrelated safety or cost claim.
worked_examples.answer: Learners currently cross the road at that location.
worked_examples.check: If no learners used that location, the stated reason would not support putting a crossing there.

common_misconceptions: A strong-sounding assumption must be relevant to the conclusion.
If P implies Q, observing Q proves P.
A rise after a policy proves the policy caused the rise.
question_patterns: State the inference in plain language before evaluating options.
Test a necessary assumption with a counterexample.
Name the denominator and comparison group for a data claim.

title: Civil Service Clerical Ability: Filing, Exact Comparison, and Proofreading
scope_note: CSC scope materials include clerical ability at the Subprofessional level, particularly filing and spelling. This guide develops careful comparison and record-control habits; consult the current CSC announcement for the examination level and scope.
learning_objectives: Apply one stated alphabetizing rule consistently.
Compare records character by character without silently correcting the source.
Proofread spelling and common sentence errors in context.

sections.heading: 1. Filing order starts with the filing key
sections.body: First identify the rule the question supplies: surname, organization name, title, or a specified filing code. Compare the first filing unit, then move character by character to the first difference. If the initial strings match, the shorter complete key normally precedes the longer one unless the stated local rule says otherwise. Treat spaces, punctuation, initials, and suffixes according to the instructions rather than inventing a convention. When an office uses a particular filing standard, follow that documented standard and record the key used so the order can be repeated.

sections.heading: 2. Compare two records without guessing
sections.body: An exact comparison asks whether two strings or records match, not whether they probably refer to the same person. Compare fields in a stable order: identifier, name, date, address, and document version. Mark the first differing character or field, then check whether the task expects exact identity, a likely match, or a spelling correction. Preserve the source value until the responsible record owner authorizes a correction. This distinction prevents a near match from being filed as a confirmed duplicate and keeps the audit trail visible.

sections.heading: 3. Spelling and proofreading in context
sections.body: Proofreading works best in deliberate passes. Read once for meaning and missing words, once for spelling and word forms, and once for punctuation or repeated material. Check a doubtful spelling against a trusted dictionary or the supplied reference; do not rely only on the visual shape of a familiar word. Context can distinguish homophones and inflected forms, but a sentence should not be “corrected” by changing its intended meaning. In clerical work, accuracy also includes reproducing names, numbers, and source wording exactly when transcription is required.

worked_examples.heading: Alphabetize a small file list
worked_examples.prompt: Which surname comes first alphabetically: Salazar, Santiago, Santos, or Sarmiento?
steps: Compare the common prefix “Sa.”
Compare the next letters: Salazar has “l”; the other names have “n” or “r.”
Since “l” precedes “n” and “r,” Salazar is first.
worked_examples.answer: Salazar.
worked_examples.check: Do not compare the first name until the filing surname is resolved.

common_misconceptions: A familiar name should be sorted by first name even when the key is surname.
Near-identical records can be treated as duplicates without checking identifiers.
Proofreading means improving the wording even when the task requires exact copying.
question_patterns: Write the filing key before comparing entries.
Mark the first exact difference in two records.
Separate correction from faithful transcription.

title: Civil Service General Information: Constitution, Ethics, Rights, and Environment
scope_note: CSC General Information scope includes the Philippine Constitution, ethical public service, human rights, and environmental protection. This is an introductory learning guide; for a legal or policy question, read the current official text and implementing issuances.
learning_objectives: Use constitutional principles as a framework for reading a civic scenario.
Apply the public-interest principle and identify a conflict that needs disclosure or review.
Distinguish a rights claim from its source and connect environmental duties to evidence.

sections.heading: 1. Constitutional structure and rights
sections.body: The Constitution establishes public institutions, distributes authority, and states rights and duties. Read a civic scenario by identifying who is acting, what authority is claimed, which person or public interest is affected, and what constitutional provision or law is relevant. Do not treat a broad principle as a substitute for the controlling text or a court’s interpretation. Rights analysis also asks what state action is involved and what process or limitation the Constitution and law provide. A disciplined answer separates the rule stated in the source from a personal view about what the rule should be.

sections.heading: 2. Public service, conflicts, and accountability
sections.body: Republic Act No. 6713 places public interest above personal interest and describes standards such as professionalism, political neutrality, responsiveness, and simple living. In a scenario, identify the official duty, the personal or outside interest, the decision affected, and the disclosure or review that protects impartial service. A conflict risk is not proof of misconduct by itself; it is a condition that must be handled under the applicable rule. A useful record names the relevant decision, responsible official, evidence, and next accountability step rather than relying on a slogan.

sections.heading: 3. Human dignity, rights, and environmental public interest
sections.body: Human-rights reasoning begins with the person or group affected, the right at issue, and the public body or actor responsible under the applicable framework. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is an international declaration; it should not be described as a Philippine statute. Environmental questions likewise require a named issue and source: air pollution, solid waste, and ecological management are addressed by different laws. Separate an observed condition from its cause, identify who can verify it, and connect the proposed response to the actual legal or policy instrument.

worked_examples.heading: Recognize a public-interest duty
worked_examples.prompt: A public employee handles a request submitted by a close friend. What is the first ethical question to resolve?
steps: Identify the employee’s official responsibility and the decision to be made.
Determine whether the relationship creates an actual or apparent personal interest under the applicable rules.
Use disclosure, reassignment, or other required safeguards rather than favoring the friend.
worked_examples.answer: The employee must protect impartial service and public interest, following the applicable disclosure and review rules.
worked_examples.check: A relationship raises a review question; the facts and governing rule determine the required action.

common_misconceptions: Every statement about rights has the same legal source or status.
A conflict of interest is automatically proof of corruption.
A general environmental concern identifies the specific law that applies.
question_patterns: Identify the actor, authority, affected person, and cited source.
Distinguish risk indicators from proven misconduct.
Use the relevant law rather than a generic civic slogan.

title: Civil Service Verbal Ability: Reading, Grammar, and Cohesion
scope_note: CSC verbal scope includes vocabulary, grammar and correct usage, paragraph organization, and reading comprehension in English and Filipino. This lesson uses original examples in both languages; it does not assume that English grammar can be transferred mechanically to Filipino.
learning_objectives: Find a passage’s central claim and distinguish it from supporting detail.
Use context to infer word meaning and evaluate a conclusion.
Apply clear sentence and paragraph relationships in English and Filipino.

sections.heading: 1. Central idea, evidence, and careful inference
sections.body: Read the question first to know whether it asks for a stated detail, central idea, inference, purpose, or evaluation. A central idea explains what the passage as a whole is doing; a detail supports one part. For inference, combine the text with the smallest necessary assumption and reject options that add facts the author never supplies. A change observed after an action does not by itself prove the action caused it. In Filipino, distinguish the pangunahing diwa from pantulong na detalye and make a hinuha that stays within the tekstong binasa.

sections.heading: 2. Vocabulary from context
sections.body: When a word is unfamiliar, reread the sentence and its neighboring sentences. Look for a definition, contrast, example, cause, or repeated idea that narrows the meaning. Substitute a candidate meaning and check whether the sentence still makes sense without changing the author’s claim. In Filipino, inspect affixes and the word’s role in the sentence, then consult a reliable Filipino dictionary when context remains ambiguous. A plausible dictionary meaning may still be wrong for this sentence if it does not fit the surrounding argument.

sections.heading: 3. Grammar as a meaning check
sections.body: For English subject–verb agreement, locate the grammatical subject rather than the nearest noun; intervening phrases do not change the subject’s number. A pronoun should have a clear antecedent and agree in number and reference. Parallel items should use matching grammatical forms. In Filipino, identify the panaguri and simuno in the actual sentence and use the appropriate pang-ugnay and word form; do not impose English agreement patterns where Filipino grammar works differently. Revision should make the intended relationship clearer, not merely sound more formal.

sections.heading: 4. Paragraph order and cohesion
sections.body: A coherent paragraph gives each sentence a job: introduce the point, explain it, support it, or connect it to the next idea. Track reference words, time markers, contrast, and cause-and-effect signals. A sentence that begins with “however” needs a genuine contrast; a pronoun should point to a clear noun; a concluding sentence should follow from the evidence already given. Test a paragraph order by reading the transitions aloud and checking whether the logic remains clear without adding an unstated premise.

worked_examples.heading: Avoid a causal overclaim
worked_examples.prompt: A report says processing time fell after a checklist was introduced, but no comparison group was used. What is the strongest conclusion?
steps: State only the observed sequence: the decrease followed introduction of the checklist.
Check whether another group or design isolates the checklist’s effect.
Avoid claiming causation when other changes remain possible.
worked_examples.answer: The result is promising, but causation is not established.
worked_examples.check: This conclusion matches the stated evidence and does not add a cause.

common_misconceptions: The longest option is always the central idea.
A temporal “after” relationship proves causation.
English grammatical categories apply identically in Filipino.
question_patterns: Label the task before reading options.
Quote or paraphrase the exact evidence supporting an inference.
Check grammar against intended meaning in the language used.

title: Advanced Accounting: Ownership, Profit Allocation, and Consolidation
scope_note: PRC has issued revised 2026 Tables of Specifications for the six LECPA subjects. This original lesson focuses on selected partnership-allocation and consolidation reasoning. Apply the current Philippine-adopted standards and the specific facts of a case; this short guide is not a complete advanced-accounting reviewer.
learning_objectives: Allocate a partnership result using the agreement’s stated priority and residual ratio.
Explain why consolidated statements treat a parent and controlled subsidiaries as one economic reporting group.
Identify intercompany items that must be examined before interpreting consolidated totals.

sections.heading: 1. Partnership agreements and profit allocation
sections.body: A partnership allocation problem is an ordered calculation, not an automatic equal split. Read the agreement for salaries, interest on capital, preferred amounts, and the residual-sharing ratio; then determine whether the stated allowances are distributions of profit or expenses in a particular accounting context. Compute the total allowances first, compare them with available profit, and allocate the remaining amount using the stated ratio. If allowances exceed the available profit, do not force a positive residual; follow the agreement’s loss or deficit rule. State every assumption so a reviewer can reproduce the allocation.

sections.heading: 2. Business combinations and control
sections.body: A business-combination analysis first identifies the acquirer and acquisition date, then considers the identifiable assets and liabilities and the consideration under the applicable standard. Consolidated reporting depends on control rather than the mere existence of an investment or a common brand. The investor assesses power over relevant activities, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use power to affect those returns under IFRS 10’s control model. Apply the standards adopted in the Philippines for the reporting period, and distinguish an acquisition calculation from later-period consolidation.

sections.heading: 3. Intercompany eliminations and foreign operations
sections.body: Consolidated statements combine like items of the parent and subsidiaries, then remove intragroup balances and transactions so the group does not report activity with itself as an external result. Identify the originating entities, transaction direction, reporting date, and whether profit remains in group assets. Foreign-operation translation adds another layer: distinguish the entity’s functional currency from the presentation currency and apply the relevant standard to assets, liabilities, income, and translation differences. These are not interchangeable topics; use the applicable IFRS requirements and source records for the specific case.

sections.heading: 4. Other advanced-accounting pathways
sections.body: Branch accounting, joint arrangements, liquidation, withdrawal, dividends, and asset transfers each require a transaction model that fits the legal arrangement and accounting policy. Begin with the parties, their rights and obligations, the reporting entity, and the event being measured. Keep a schedule that reconciles opening balances, current activity, allocations, eliminations, and ending balances. This broad introduction does not teach the recognition details of every pathway; consult the current LECPA TOS and applicable Philippine-adopted standards before treating a topic as covered.

worked_examples.heading: Allocate partnership profit
worked_examples.prompt: A partnership earns ₱360,000. A receives a ₱120,000 salary allowance and B ₱80,000; capital interest is 10% on ₱400,000 and ₱200,000, respectively; the residual is shared 3:2. Find A’s total allocation.
steps: Salary allowances total ₱200,000; capital-interest allowances are ₱40,000 and ₱20,000, so total allowances are ₱260,000.
A receives 3/5 of the residual, or ₱60,000; add A’s salary ₱120,000 and interest ₱40,000.
worked_examples.answer: A’s total allocation is ₱220,000.
worked_examples.check: The partners receive ₱360,000 in total: ₱220,000 for A and ₱140,000 for B.

common_misconceptions: Salary or interest allowances are always operating expenses.
An investment automatically gives its holder control.
Consolidation means adding every ledger balance without eliminations.
question_patterns: Read the agreement before calculating allocations.
Separate acquisition-date analysis from later reporting.
Reconcile intercompany balances before interpreting group results.

title: Financial Accounting: Recognition, Measurement, and Reporting Checks
scope_note: The current PRC LECPA TOS is the official scope reference. This lesson organizes selected accrual, measurement, presentation, and analysis methods; use the Philippine-adopted version and effective date of each standard for a reporting period. It does not replace the standards text.
learning_objectives: Apply accrual timing to expenses and unearned/earned customer amounts.
Distinguish recognition from measurement and presentation.
Use reconciliation checks when interpreting financial-statement effects.

sections.heading: 1. Accruals, cut-off, and customer advances
sections.body: Accrual accounting records the economic event in the period it occurs, subject to the applicable recognition requirements, rather than simply following cash movement. An incurred but unpaid utility expense belongs to the period of use; an expired portion of prepaid insurance is an expense; a customer advance remains a liability until the relevant performance or earning conditions are met. At period end, identify the service or right received, the time interval, supporting documents, and whether an amount is earned, incurred, paid, or still deferred. Cut-off errors often arise when these states are treated as synonyms.

sections.heading: 2. Assets, inventory, revenue, and measurement
sections.body: Recognition asks whether an item belongs in the statements under the applicable standard; measurement asks which amount and subsequent measurement basis apply. Inventory, property and equipment, revenue, leases, and financial instruments each have their own criteria and measurement mechanics. Do not generalize one standard’s model across every asset or contract. Trace the transaction from contract or purchase evidence to the account, estimate, and note disclosure; verify the current adopted text and effective date. A carrying amount is not automatically recoverable simply because it was recorded at cost, and revenue timing follows the relevant performance obligations rather than cash collection alone.

sections.heading: 3. Estimates, impairment, and cash-flow interpretation
sections.body: Estimates use available evidence at a measurement date and may need revision when conditions or information change. A provision requires the criteria in the applicable standard; uncertainty alone does not justify recording any desired reserve. An impairment assessment compares carrying amounts with the measure required by the relevant standard and unit of account. Cash-flow analysis then reconciles opening and closing cash through operating, investing, and financing activity, while keeping noncash transactions separate. Tie reported changes back to ledgers, disclosures, and prior-period comparatives before drawing a conclusion about performance or liquidity.

sections.heading: 4. Presentation and a reviewable audit trail
sections.body: Financial statements tell a connected story: assets and liabilities at a date, income and expenses over a period, and cash movements across that period. Classification and presentation should follow the standard and reporting context rather than a convenient ratio. Maintain a trail from source document to journal entry, calculation schedule, general ledger, statement line, and disclosure. When two sources disagree, resolve the underlying fact and document the judgment; do not force the ledger to match an unsupported expectation.

worked_examples.heading: Separate expenses from earned revenue
worked_examples.prompt: At reporting date, utilities incurred are ₱18,000, insurance expired is ₱7,000, and a ₱12,000 customer deposit has been earned. What expense is recognized from the first two items?
steps: Identify utilities as incurred expense: ₱18,000.
Identify expired insurance as the used portion: ₱7,000.
Add only the expense amounts; the customer deposit affects revenue, not this expense total.
worked_examples.answer: Recognized expense is ₱25,000.
worked_examples.check: Cash payment timing does not change the stated incurrence or expiry facts.

common_misconceptions: Cash received always means revenue has been earned.
An estimate is an arbitrary reserve rather than a supportable measurement.
A financial-statement total can be checked without its source and period.
question_patterns: Name the reporting period and economic event.
Keep recognition, measurement, and presentation as separate questions.
Trace the number from evidence through ledger to disclosure.

title: Management Services: Contribution, Break-Even, and Decision Models
scope_note: PRC’s 2026 revised LECPA TOS governs official subject coverage. This lesson teaches selected internal planning tools using stated assumptions; its hypothetical figures do not represent Philippine tax, financial-reporting, or business advice.
learning_objectives: Compute unit contribution and break-even volume.
Explain the assumptions and relevant range behind a CVP result.
Compare a decision using relevant costs and state nonfinancial constraints.

sections.heading: 1. Contribution margin and break-even
sections.body: For one product under a linear cost-volume-profit model, unit contribution margin equals selling price per unit less variable cost per unit. Fixed cost divided by unit contribution gives break-even units; fixed cost divided by contribution-margin ratio gives break-even sales dollars. At break-even, total contribution exactly covers fixed cost and operating income is zero. Keep units and currency consistent, and distinguish the contribution from gross margin or cash flow. For a multi-product setting, a weighted mix assumption matters because products may have different contribution margins.

sections.heading: 2. Test assumptions and sensitivity
sections.body: CVP results are conditional estimates. Common simplifying assumptions include a stable selling price, linear variable cost, fixed cost within a relevant range, and known sales mix. A change in capacity, overtime, discounting, product mix, or inventory can break those assumptions. Sensitivity analysis changes one or more inputs transparently and recomputes contribution and break-even; it does not guarantee the forecast. A margin-of-safety measure compares expected or actual sales with break-even, and operating leverage describes how a change in sales can affect operating income under the modeled cost structure.

sections.heading: 3. Relevant costs, budgets, and variance questions
sections.body: A decision-relevant cost differs between alternatives and relates to a future consequence. A sunk cost is already incurred and cannot be changed by the current choice, while an avoidable future cost may matter. Compare alternatives on consistent units and horizon, then include capacity, quality, delivery, safety, and strategic constraints that the arithmetic omits. Budget variances are signals to investigate: define the benchmark, actual measure, flexible volume basis, and cause before calling a variance favorable or unfavorable. Responsibility accounting should focus on items a manager can reasonably influence.

worked_examples.heading: Find break-even volume
worked_examples.prompt: A product sells for ₱80, has variable cost ₱50, and fixed cost ₱240,000. Find break-even volume under the one-product linear model.
steps: Unit contribution = ₱80 − ₱50 = ₱30 per unit.
Break-even units = fixed cost ÷ unit contribution = ₱240,000 ÷ ₱30.
Check revenue and total cost at that volume.
worked_examples.answer: 8,000 units.
worked_examples.check: Sales are ₱640,000; variable costs are ₱400,000; contribution of ₱240,000 covers fixed cost exactly.

common_misconceptions: Break-even is reliable outside the stated relevant range.
Fixed cost per unit remains fixed as volume changes.
A favorable variance automatically reflects good management.
question_patterns: Write the assumptions before calculating break-even.
Label contribution per unit and total contribution separately.
Investigate the cause and controllability of a variance.

title: CPA Regulatory Framework: Authority, Ethics, Contracts, and Audit Evidence
scope_note: The PRC Board of Accountancy publishes current LECPA TOS and Philippine professional issuances. This introductory lesson teaches source-checking and selected legal/audit reasoning; law and standards change, and the current primary text and effective date govern an actual professional decision.
learning_objectives: Identify which primary authority and date control a regulatory question.
Analyze a basic contract sequence from the facts given without inventing missing terms.
Explain why audit evidence must address the relevant assertion and risk.

sections.heading: 1. Professional authority and ethical duties
sections.body: Start a regulatory question by naming the profession, the act or decision, the authority responsible, and the date relevant to the case. Republic Act No. 9298 establishes the Philippine accountancy regulatory framework; PRC and Board of Accountancy resolutions, applicable laws, and professional pronouncements provide additional requirements within their scope. Ethical analysis identifies the fundamental principle at risk, the relevant relationship or pressure, and safeguards required by the applicable Philippine Code of Ethics. A general ethical value is not a substitute for the actual rule, independence requirement, or effective date.

sections.heading: 2. Contract questions: order the facts, then check the rule
sections.body: For a contract problem, write the dated sequence of offer, acceptance, communication, revocation, and any stated condition. Then consult the relevant Civil Code provisions and determine which act was legally effective and when. Do not assume a time limit, delivery method, or jurisdiction-specific deadline unless the problem or source supplies it. The distinction between dispatch and receipt can matter for communications. If an essential fact is missing, state the conditional conclusion rather than filling the gap with an unstated rule. This method makes an answer traceable and protects against overconfident legal generalization.

sections.heading: 3. Corporate authority and entity evidence
sections.body: Corporate analysis begins by identifying the entity, its governing documents, the decision-maker, and the act at issue. The Revised Corporation Code distinguishes corporate forms and assigns requirements for organizational and governance acts; special laws may also apply. For an accounting or audit task, connect a recorded transaction to minutes, contracts, ownership records, bank evidence, or other relevant documentation. A corporate record is evidence to evaluate, not proof by title alone. Check amendments and current SEC rules before advising on a live corporate act.

sections.heading: 4. Audit standards and assertion-directed evidence
sections.body: Audit procedures should respond to assessed risk and the assertion being tested, such as existence, completeness, valuation, rights and obligations, or presentation. Evidence quality depends on relevance and reliability in context; one document may support one assertion while leaving another untested. Read the applicable Philippine Auditing Standard, including its effective date and adoption source, before treating a procedure as required. A sample reconciliation or analytical procedure is a learning example, not a complete audit program or assurance conclusion.

worked_examples.heading: Order offer, revocation, and acceptance
worked_examples.prompt: An offer is communicated January 10, revocation January 12, and acceptance January 13. What conclusion follows from the stated sequence for this exercise?
steps: Write the sequence in order: offer, revocation, acceptance.
The stated revocation precedes the stated acceptance.
Do not add an unstated deadline or communication rule; consult the applicable Civil Code provisions for a real case.
worked_examples.answer: Under the facts and assumptions supplied in the exercise, no contract formed because revocation preceded acceptance.
worked_examples.check: The reasoning depends on the exercise’s facts and does not decide questions of notice or effective receipt that were not supplied.

common_misconceptions: A PRC webpage title proves every later amendment is in force.
A legal conclusion can ignore when a communication became effective.
A document is persuasive evidence for every audit assertion.
question_patterns: Record the authority, section, version, and effective date.
Sequence legal events before applying a rule.
Tie each audit procedure to a stated risk and assertion.

title: Taxation: Computation Workflow and Current-Law Verification
scope_note: The PRC 2026 LECPA TOS is the exam-scope source. Philippine tax rules, rates, filing duties, and BIR issuances are time-sensitive. This lesson teaches a calculation workflow and uses only rates or treatments explicitly supplied in a hypothetical problem; it does not state a current tax rate or provide tax advice.
learning_objectives: Separate facts, tax base, treatment, rate, and liability in a tax problem.
Compute a base from a supplied schedule without importing an unstated rate.
Verify a current requirement in the applicable law and BIR issuance.

sections.heading: 1. Begin with the taxpayer, transaction, and source date
sections.body: Before calculating, identify the taxpayer, tax type, transaction date, place, accounting period, and facts that affect classification. Then locate the controlling provision in the National Internal Revenue Code as amended and the applicable BIR regulation, revenue memorandum, or other issuance. Check publication, effectivity, amendments, transition rules, and whether the source covers this taxpayer and transaction. A summary page or old reviewer can help you find a provision but cannot establish a current rate or deadline. Preserve the source and date behind each assumption in the computation.

sections.heading: 2. Build a tax base from stated components
sections.body: A tax-base calculation begins with the gross amount identified by the problem, then applies only inclusions, exclusions, deductions, credits, or adjustments that are supported by the stated facts and governing rule. Keep separate columns for the source amount, treatment, rule citation, and arithmetic. A permitted cost may reduce a base only if it qualifies under the applicable rules and evidence; the word “cost” by itself does not prove deductibility. When an examination item supplies a tax schedule, use the supplied treatment for that exercise and label the result as conditional on that schedule.

sections.heading: 3. Indirect taxes, documentation, and compliance
sections.body: Indirect-tax problems may turn on transaction type, place of supply, registration, exemptions, timing, documentation, and the rule effective on the transaction date. Separate output tax, input tax, tax-inclusive amounts, and cash remittance rather than combining them prematurely. BIR issuances can implement statutory changes and contain transition details, so confirm the exact issuance and its status. For filing and payment, verify the current form, channel, due date, and taxpayer category with an official BIR source. A worked classroom amount does not establish a real person’s filing obligation.

sections.heading: 4. Review and reconcile the computation
sections.body: A reviewable computation exposes its assumptions, units, tax period, rate source, rounding rule, and supporting records. Recalculate the base independently, reconcile it to books or source documents, and test whether each adjustment is included once. Separate a book-to-tax adjustment from a cash payment and from a return line. If a required rule or fact is missing, identify that gap rather than filling it from memory. For a live transaction, the responsible professional must verify current law and case facts before relying on a study example.

worked_examples.heading: Compute a base using a supplied schedule
worked_examples.prompt: A hypothetical exercise states receipts of ₱500,000 and allowable costs of ₱180,000 under its supplied schedule. What base remains before any further adjustments?
steps: Use only the treatment supplied for the exercise.
Subtract the stated allowable costs: ₱500,000 − ₱180,000.
Label the result as the exercise base before other adjustments.
worked_examples.answer: ₱320,000 under the supplied hypothetical schedule.
worked_examples.check: This arithmetic does not establish that those costs are deductible under current Philippine tax law.

common_misconceptions: A historical reviewer’s rate remains current by default.
Every recorded business cost is automatically deductible.
A taxable base is the same as the final tax liability.
question_patterns: Identify tax type, person, transaction date, and period.
Cite the exact source for every treatment and rate.
Reconcile adjustments and disclose missing facts.

title: LET English: Reading Evidence, Grammar, and Composition
scope_note: Use PRC’s current LEPT TOS and alignment issuances for exam scope. DepEd’s K–12 English guide supports the curriculum competencies represented here. This original lesson covers selected language and reading skills; it is not a complete English specialization guide.
learning_objectives: Infer a conclusion from a short passage while respecting its evidence limits.
Explain how grammar and reference choices affect meaning.
Organize a short response around a clear claim and supporting evidence.

sections.heading: 1. Read a claim through its evidence
sections.body: A reader should distinguish what a passage states, what it suggests, and what remains unknown. Identify the central claim, the evidence offered, and the connection between them. Then ask whether the evidence actually supports the conclusion or merely occurs at the same time. In teaching and assessment, a response that cites relevant details and explains their connection is stronger than one that repeats a claim without evidence. Use an original passage as a shared text, then ask learners to justify one inference and identify an alternative explanation.

sections.heading: 2. Grammar, agreement, and clear reference
sections.body: When revising a sentence, locate its main subject and verb, then check whether their forms agree. A phrase between subject and verb may be informative but does not normally become the subject. Pronouns need an identifiable antecedent and a clear number reference; modifiers should sit close to what they describe. A grammatical correction should preserve the intended proposition. Read the revised sentence in context to make sure a local edit has not changed the writer’s meaning or obscured the relationship between ideas.

sections.heading: 3. Vocabulary, purpose, and text structure
sections.body: Use context clues as evidence rather than as a guess: nearby definitions, examples, contrasts, and cause-and-effect relationships narrow a word’s meaning. Text structure can signal whether a writer is comparing ideas, explaining a sequence, or describing a problem and response. Purpose and tone should be inferred from the whole passage, including word choice and the intended audience. A single loaded word is not enough to label the tone if the rest of the passage points elsewhere.

sections.heading: 4. Composition, cohesion, and feedback
sections.body: A useful paragraph makes one claim, supports it with relevant detail, and explains why that detail matters. Cohesion comes from clear reference, logical sequencing, and transitions that accurately express the relationship between sentences. In a classroom response, feedback should point to the evidence or sentence move that needs revision and give the learner a chance to try again. A polished surface is not enough if the paragraph’s reasoning is unsupported; likewise, a useful draft can be improved without erasing the writer’s voice.

worked_examples.heading: Read a finding without overclaiming
worked_examples.prompt: Learners compared two explanations using the same evidence, and most revised their original claim. What does this show?
steps: Identify the observed action: learners compared explanations against evidence.
Identify the observed response: most revised their initial claim.
Avoid claiming that they permanently mastered the concept or that comparison alone caused the change.
worked_examples.answer: The activity prompted evidence-based reconsideration rather than simple recall.
worked_examples.check: The conclusion describes the observed reasoning behavior without making a causal or mastery claim.

common_misconceptions: A single sentence can always establish a passage’s purpose.
A grammar edit is correct even if it changes the intended meaning.
A revised response proves durable learning without later evidence.
question_patterns: Point to the exact sentence or detail supporting an inference.
Check the main subject and antecedent before revising.
Give feedback that names a next step the learner can perform.

title: LET Filipino: Pagbasa, Wastong Gamit, at Pagbuo ng Teksto
scope_note: Ang saklaw ay ibabatay sa kasalukuyang PRC LEPT TOS at sa mga sanggunian ng DepEd at Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino. Orihinal ang mga paliwanag at halimbawa rito. Panimulang yunit lamang ito, hindi buong reviewer sa Filipino.
learning_objectives: Matukoy ang pangunahing diwa at ebidensiya sa tekstong binasa.
Makabuo ng hinuha na hindi lumalampas sa impormasyong nasa teksto.
Maipaliwanag kung paanong ang gramatika, talasalitaan, at organisasyon ay lumilinaw sa kahulugan.

sections.heading: 1. Pangunahing diwa at ebidensiya
sections.body: Basahin muna kung ang tanong ay tungkol sa tuwirang detalye, pangunahing diwa, layunin, o hinuha. Ang pangunahing diwa ang ideyang pinag-uugnay ng mahahalagang pangungusap; hindi ito basta pinakamadalas na salitang lumilitaw. Itala ang detalyeng sumusuporta rito at suriin kung talagang pinatutunayan ng detalye ang pahayag. Kapag may dalawang pagbabagong naganap kasabay ng pagtaas o pagbaba, huwag magtakda agad ng iisang sanhi kung walang paghahambing na naghihiwalay sa epekto.

sections.heading: 2. Hinuha mula sa konteksto
sections.body: Ang hinuha ay konklusyong binubuo mula sa tekstuwal na pahiwatig at makatwirang ugnayan; hindi ito opinyong walang batayan. Hanapin ang pahayag, halimbawa, pangatnig, at kundisyong inilalahad ng may-akda. Pagkatapos, sabihin kung ano ang ipinahihiwatig at kung anong impormasyon ang hindi pa tiyak. Para sa salitang di-pamilyar, gamitin ang depinisyon, paghahambing, kasalungat, o halimbawa sa paligid nito. Kung may maraming posibleng kahulugan, tingnan ang gamit nito sa pangungusap at sumangguni sa mapagkakatiwalaang diksiyonaryo.

sections.heading: 3. Wastong gamit, gramatika, at estruktura
sections.body: Suriin ang gampanin ng bawat salita sa pangungusap bago pumili ng anyo o pang-ugnay. Tingnan kung malinaw ang simuno at panaguri, kung ang panghalip ay may tiyak na tinutukoy, at kung lohikal ang ugnayan ng mga sugnay. Ang wastong gamit ay nakabatay sa kahulugan at tuntunin sa Filipino, hindi sa tuwirang paglilipat ng tuntunin sa Ingles. Gamitin ang Balarila at iba pang sanggunian bilang batayan, ngunit isaalang-alang din ang rehistro, konteksto, at layunin ng pahayag.

sections.heading: 4. Panitikan at organisadong pagsulat
sections.body: Sa pagsusuri ng akda, ihiwalay ang nakikitang detalye sa interpretasyon: sino ang nagsasalaysay, ano ang nagaganap, anong tunggalian ang lumilitaw, at anong tema ang sinusuportahan ng mga pangyayari. Isaalang-alang ang panahon, pamayanan, at pananaw nang hindi ipinapalagay na iisa ang karanasan ng lahat. Sa buod, piliin lamang ang mahahalagang ideya at panatilihin ang ugnayan ng mga ito; huwag magdagdag ng bagong paghuhusga. Sa talatang nagpapaliwanag, ayusin ang pahayag, patunay, at paliwanag sa lohikal na pagkakasunod-sunod.

worked_examples.heading: Maingat na hinuha sa Filipino
worked_examples.prompt: Tumaas ang pagdalo matapos ang paalala, ngunit kasabay nito ay nagbago ang iskedyul. Ano ang pinakamaingat na hinuha?
steps: Itala ang dalawang pagbabagong kasabay ng pagtaas: paalala at iskedyul.
Suriin kung may paghahambing na naghihiwalay sa epekto ng bawat pagbabago.
Piliin ang konklusyong nagsasabi lamang ng nasusuportahan ng tala.
worked_examples.answer: Tumaas ang pagdalo kasabay ng dalawang pagbabago; hindi matitiyak ang hiwalay na epekto.
worked_examples.check: Hindi tinutukoy ng tala kung alin sa dalawang pagbabago ang sanhi ng pagtaas.

common_misconceptions: Ang pangunahing diwa ay kapareho ng isang detalyeng kawili-wili.
Ang hinuha ay maaaring magdagdag ng impormasyong wala sa teksto.
Maaaring ipalit nang direkta sa Filipino ang tuntunin sa Ingles.
question_patterns: Tukuyin ang uri ng tanong bago pumili ng sagot.
Iugnay ang hinuha sa tiyak na pahiwatig.
Ihiwalay ang buod, interpretasyon, at sariling opinyon.

title: LET Mathematics: Number Sense, Models, and Data Reasoning
scope_note: The PRC LEPT TOS and DepEd Mathematics curriculum are the scope references. This lesson teaches selected quantitative reasoning with original numbers; check the current curriculum and examination documents before treating it as a complete specialization guide.
learning_objectives: Choose an operation and representation that fits a word problem.
Solve and check a one-variable equation or proportional relationship.
Summarize and compare data using the correct unit and baseline.

sections.heading: 1. Number sense, operations, and units
sections.body: Estimate before calculating so an answer with an impossible sign or scale is easy to notice. Keep the unit attached to each quantity and convert to a common unit before adding or comparing. Fractions, decimals, and percentages are alternate representations of a relationship; choose the one that makes the calculation transparent. In multi-step problems, state what each intermediate value represents instead of copying numbers into an unexplained expression. A reasonable estimate and a reverse check can reveal errors that a calculator will not.

sections.heading: 2. Equations, patterns, and functions
sections.body: Translate a verbal condition into an equation by naming the unknown and defining each term. Solve with equivalent operations, then substitute the result into the original statement. A pattern suggests a rule; verify the rule against every given term before extending it. A function describes how an output depends on an input under a defined relationship, and a graph can show where the relationship rises, falls, or changes. Distinguish a model’s prediction from an observed measurement, and state the range where the model makes sense.

sections.heading: 3. Geometry and measurement
sections.body: Geometry problems are easier when you draw and label the figure before selecting a formula. Identify the requested quantity—length, perimeter, area, angle, or volume—and check that the formula matches the shape. Use the stated units consistently and remember that area uses square units. A diagram may not be drawn to scale, so use the given measurements and relationships rather than visual appearance. For angle or shape relationships, write the rule that connects the parts and test whether the values meet the full condition.

sections.heading: 4. Summaries, probability, and data
sections.body: Before summarizing a data set, identify the population or sample, variable, and unit of observation. The mean uses all values and can move under an extreme observation; the median is the middle ordered value and may better represent a skewed set. Probability describes a defined event within a stated sample space; it is not a guarantee about one outcome. When comparing totals or rates, use the same time window and denominator. Explain what the data support and avoid extending the result to a population or cause that was not studied.

worked_examples.heading: Compare time totals
worked_examples.prompt: Reading takes 30, 40, and 35 minutes over three days; practice takes 20, 15, and 25 minutes; review takes 10, 15, and 20 minutes. Which total is largest, and by how much over the second largest?
steps: Reading: 30 + 40 + 35 = 105 minutes.
Compare the totals and subtract 105 − 60 = 45.
worked_examples.answer: Reading is largest, by 45 minutes over practice.
worked_examples.check: All three totals use the same unit and three-day period.

common_misconceptions: An answer that looks reasonable needs no unit or reverse check.
A graph’s visual scale replaces the values and labels.
The mean and median always describe a data set equally well.
question_patterns: Name the unknown and units before writing an equation.
Check a solution in the original condition.
Compare like units, periods, and denominators.
